action: Companies serving California residents: test that your sites honour opt-out preference signals, remove extra steps from opt-out flows, disclose how signals are processed, and review new tracking technologies before deployment.
exec: California continues to enforce its privacy law with fines; companies handling residents' data face real penalties.
plain: California's privacy agency fined car rental company Hertz $1.55 million for not honouring people's requests to stop the sale or sharing of their data.

key_findings: The fine is $1.55 million under the California Consumer Privacy Act, per coverage of the agency's statement.
Hertz allegedly did not process opt-out preference signals or disclose how it handled them.
The agency also alleged added friction in the opt-out process and failure to honour opt-out requests.
The number of consumers affected is not given in the coverage read.
recommendations: Process opt-out preference signals and disclose how they are handled.
Test opt-out compliance and monitor it quarterly.
Review all new tracking technologies before deployment.

summary: The California Privacy Protection Agency fined Hertz $1.55 million, according to The Record's report of the agency's statement. Alleged failings were not processing opt-out preference signals, not disclosing how signals were handled, adding friction to opting out and not honouring opt-out requests. Hertz agreed to quarterly testing and monitoring and to review new tracking technologies. The agency's own announcement would not load.
title: California privacy agency fines Hertz $1.55 million under state privacy law

validation.note: The Record article read in full; the CalPrivacy announcement redirected and did not load.
